testo: A guarded aerospace site.
A drone heads for it, confirmed about nine hundred and fifty metres out: in time for the operator.
What should the screen say when no sensor sees it?
Mowvee gives every track one of three answers.
I see it.
I don't see it: here is where it can be.
Or: I don't know.
In simulation, it says empty only where it has looked, if the site map is right.
A possible-presence warning stays on until the whole zone is checked, or the object is seen again.
Radar, LiDAR, cameras, and aircraft and drone broadcasts: all simulated from public data sheets.
Where a sensor cannot see a drone, the zone stays unverified.
Dense fog.
Mowvee declares each sensor's reach.
For a small drone, radar range drops from one thousand and sixty-two to one thousand and forty-one metres: a small change, not an independent check.
Two drones collide.
Mowvee infers the event two point two seconds later; within two seconds in fifty-one runs of sixty.
A debris zone opens.
It grows, does not shrink by looking, and cannot tell who is at risk.
An engine fails on the take-off run, with a flash.
Mowvee declares the blinded cameras unreliable, within three cycles in every simulated run.
Only the radar is left: here it loses the aircraft for seconds at a time, and Mowvee says so.
The debris warning does not discriminate: about ninety-six tracks per run.
First, the limits.
No physical sensor: all simulated.
Almost half the values are assumed.
Classes are labelled by hand.
For aircraft in flight, warnings come too late.
A drone that stops can slip out of the warning: twelve runs of two hundred.
What holds, in simulation: a drone on the site was announced in time in all two hundred runs, and its position never declared empty, with the site map declared complete.
The same core, from our short-range version: a person behind an obstacle, a depth camera, the same three answers.
Mowvee.
Seen, not seen, unknown: declared for every track.
It observes and warns.
No output is a command.
By S D M S.
